intro:
These exercises train one discipline: treat the GPU as a throughput device guarded by an expensive boundary, and prove that boundary pays for itself before any kernel ships. You start by choosing among CPU, Rayon, MPI, and CUDA from the shape of the workload, then count the bytes that actually cross the bus, then build the safe Rust wrapper that validates shape and launch configuration before one small unsafe launch. The later exercises move up the stack: repairing a tiny-kernel service that lost to the CPU, reading a profile to find the dominant cost category, and integrating a single device into an async and distributed service as a scarce shared worker.

The through-line is that almost every GPU failure in service code is a systems mistake wearing a performance costume. The kernel is rarely the problem. The trouble is too many small launches, too much copying, a borrowed buffer that outlived its request, or one shared device with no admission control. The answers below keep returning to arithmetic intensity, to transfer and launch amortization, and to the ownership story that lets Rust keep the host side of the boundary honest.

exerciseSolutions.title: Choose CPU, Rayon, MPI, or CUDA from the workload
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Map each workload to the execution model whose dominant cost it actually pays, not to whichever tool sounds most powerful. The single number that predicts a GPU win is arithmetic intensity: how much math you do per byte you move across the bus. Pair that with batch size and the level at which the real partition lives (host memory, one node, or many nodes), and each workload sorts cleanly.

The tiny request-local transform over one 4 KB buffer stays on the CPU. There is almost no arithmetic to do, the data is small, and a host-to-device copy plus a launch plus a synchronize plus a copy back would cost far more than running the transform inline. This is a low-intensity, low-volume job; the accelerator boundary would dominate the entire request.

The one-node dense batch score over host memory wants Rayon. The data already lives in one address space on one machine, the work is embarrassingly parallel across rows, and you can saturate the cores with a parallel iterator without ever leaving host memory or paying a transfer. There is no partition to ship across a network and no boundary to amortize, so the cheapest parallelism is the data-parallel CPU path.

The multi-node domain-decomposed solver wants MPI because the dominant partition is already process-level. The problem is split across machines by domain, the bottleneck is the halo exchange between ranks, and the natural unit of work is one process per subdomain communicating with its neighbors. Reaching for a GPU here would not address the real cost, which is inter-process communication, not single-node math throughput.

The dense batched tensor operation with high arithmetic intensity wants CUDA. Dense batched math does a large amount of computation per byte transferred, so the kernel runs long enough to hide the host-device copies behind it and the launch overhead is amortized across a big batch. This is the one case where the bus cost is paid back many times over by the arithmetic, which is the justification the GPU case actually requires.
criteria: CPU for the 4 KB transform, Rayon for the one-node batch score, MPI for the domain-decomposed solver, CUDA for the dense batched tensor op covers all four targets.
The CUDA case is justified by the kernel running long enough to amortize transfer and launch, not by the word 'parallel'.
CPU-bound work (the math itself) is kept distinct from waiting-bound work (the inter-process halo exchange that drives the MPI choice).

exerciseSolutions.title: Estimate transfer cost before discussing the kernel
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Count the bytes on the bus before tuning any arithmetic; the transfer is a fixed cost that never appears in a kernel-only profile. One f32 matrix of 4096 by 4096 has 4096 * 4096 = 16,777,216 elements, and each f32 is 4 bytes, so one matrix occupies 16,777,216 * 4 = 67,108,864 bytes, which is 64 MiB.

The call transfers A and B to the device and copies C back once. That is three matrix-sized transfers in total: two host-to-device plus one device-to-host. Total traffic is 3 * 67,108,864 = 201,326,592 bytes, which is 192 MiB. The transfer_bytes helper in the chapter's transfer-budget sample computes exactly this shape: elements times the f32 size times the count of input plus output buffers.

This boundary is far less painful for GEMM than for a tiny vector add because of arithmetic intensity. A dense 4096-cubed matrix multiply does on the order of 2 * 4096^3, roughly 1.4e11 floating-point operations, against about 2e8 bytes moved. That is hundreds of FLOPs per byte, so the kernel runs long enough to hide the copies behind it and the 192 MiB transfer is paid back many times over. A vector add, by contrast, does one add per several bytes moved, is memory-bandwidth-limited, and is acutely transfer-sensitive, so the same boundary swamps the work.

Transfer is not the only fixed cost, though. Launch overhead and synchronization remain separate categories: every kernel launch costs a fixed amount regardless of size, and waiting for the device to finish before copying C back is its own stall. For a single large GEMM these are negligible relative to the math, but they are the costs that dominate when a service launches many tiny kernels, so they belong on the ledger as their own line items.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One matrix is 64 MiB; the full A,B in / C out round trip is 192 MiB on the bus.
criteria: The traffic total is computed as 201,326,592 bytes (192 MiB) from three 64 MiB matrices.
The amortization argument cites GEMM's hundreds of FLOPs per byte versus vector add's bandwidth-limited one-op-per-few-bytes.
Launch and synchronization overhead are named as separate cost categories from the copy traffic.

exerciseSolutions.title: Sketch a safe Rust wrapper around a launch boundary
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Put every invariant in the safe wrapper and shrink the unsafe region to the launch itself. This is the same wrapper discipline the book uses around FFI: the GPU boundary is not special, so the checks belong in ordinary safe Rust and the unsafe block does nothing but the call it cannot avoid.

validate_buffers rejects the two failure modes that would otherwise become silent device-side corruption. It returns Err for any zero-length buffer, because a zero-length launch is a launch with nothing to do, and it returns Err when the three lengths disagree, because mismatched shapes are the classic out-of-bounds the safe layer exists to prevent. It returns Result rather than a bare bool so the caller learns which invariant failed and can propagate it with the question mark operator, the same way the chapter's build_launch_config returns Err("empty input") and Err("threads_per_block must be > 0").

build_config computes the grid from the data, not from a hard-coded guess. Blocks is the ceiling division ((len + tpb - 1) / tpb) so the grid covers every element including a ragged final block, and it is zero when threads_per_block is zero, which the raw launch then refuses. That mirrors the chapter sample exactly: grid and block shape are derived and checked before the raw launch becomes even possible.

The unsafe region stays smaller than the validation around it. By the time control reaches the unsafe launch, lengths are equal and nonzero, the block and thread counts are nonzero, and the SAFETY comment can state those facts plainly so another engineer re-derives the invariants in a few seconds. The ownership story is the point: the host wrapper owns the device buffers, decides when they exist, and guarantees they outlive the launch, which is precisely the discipline that keeps a mismatched length from becoming undefined behavior.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: All shape and grid invariants are checked in safe code; the unsafe block only performs the launch.
criteria: validate_buffers runs and must succeed before the unsafe call is reached.
build_config derives block count from len and threads_per_block with ceiling division.
The checked boundary returns Result<LaunchConfig, &'static str>, not a vague boolean.
The runnable lab prints blocks = 8, threads = 128, launch ok = true.

exerciseSolutions.title: Repair a tiny-kernel service path that lost to the CPU
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Diagnose the path as launch-bound and transfer-bound, then fix it in the cheapest order. The service copies one small vector, launches one tiny kernel, synchronizes immediately, copies the result back, and repeats that whole cycle per request item. This is the fastest wrong architecture in the chapter: per-item it pays a full host-device round trip and a launch and a synchronize for an arithmetic payload too small to amortize any of them.

The first fix is batching, not kernel rewriting. Accumulate many request items into one large buffer and launch a single kernel over the batch, so one transfer and one launch and one synchronize cover thousands of items instead of one. Batching alone collapses both the launch count and the per-item copy overhead, which are the two costs actually dominating here. Fusing adjacent kernels is the natural second move once batching is in place, because it removes intermediate device-to-host round trips between stages; reusing persistent device buffers across batches is the third, since it stops re-allocating the same scratch on every call. Kernel-level tuning is last, because the kernel was never the bottleneck.

The signal that the path is launch-bound rather than kernel-bound is the relationship between launch count and kernel time. If a profile shows a high launch count with each kernel finishing in microseconds while wall time is dominated by queue wait and copy time, the device is spending its day on admission and transfer, not arithmetic. Concretely: kernel time is a small fraction of wall time, launches scale one-to-one with request items, and per-launch fixed overhead times the launch count approaches the total. That is launch-bound; shaving FLOPs would not move wall time.

The best repair is sometimes to not use the GPU at all for this route. If the per-item work stays small and cannot be batched, because items arrive one at a time with a tight latency budget and no opportunity to coalesce, the transfer and launch will always dominate and the CPU path will keep winning. The CPU fallback condition is exactly that: when arithmetic intensity is low and batch size cannot grow, run it inline on the host and reserve the device for routes that can fill a batch.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Batch first when work is launch-bound and batchable; fall back to CPU when items cannot be coalesced.
criteria: Batching is named as the first repair and an un-batchable, low-intensity route is named as the CPU fallback condition.
The path is explained through transfer, launch, and synchronization overhead rather than 'GPU is faster'.
Launch count, queue wait, and per-launch kernel time are cited as the profiling signals that identify launch-bound behavior.

exerciseSolutions.title: Profile a CUDA workload before rewriting the kernel
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Break the 24 ms wall time into named stages and diagnose from the largest one, not from the kernel. The report gives kernel 2 ms, host-device copies 11 ms, queue wait 6 ms, and total 24 ms. Kernel math is only 2 of 24 ms, about 8 percent; copies are 11 ms and queue wait is 6 ms, which together are 17 ms, roughly 70 percent of the wall time. The remaining few milliseconds are launch and synchronization slack.

The dominant category is transfer and admission, not kernel arithmetic. Copies at 11 ms are the single largest stage and the queue wait at 6 ms says requests are also spending real time before the device even accepts them. The first diagnosis is that this batch scorer is transfer-bound with a secondary admission problem, and the kernel is comfortably the cheapest part of the round trip.

The premature rewrite is low-level kernel tuning. Optimizing instruction selection, occupancy, or shared-memory layout would attack the 2 ms stage and, even if it halved kernel time, would shave at most about 1 ms off a 24 ms wall time. That is the classic mistake the chapter warns against: a kernel-only profile cannot tell you whether you are transfer-bound, and here the rest of the report says plainly that you are. Kernel tuning is the wrong first target.

The next measurement is inside the transfer category. Split the 11 ms of copies into host-to-device and device-to-host, and check whether inputs are being re-sent each call when they could be resident on the device, and whether the copies overlap with compute or serialize against it. If inputs are static, cache them on the device and stream only the per-request payload; if copies serialize, move to pinned host memory and asynchronous copies so transfer and kernel overlap. In parallel, measure batch size against the queue to see whether the 6 ms wait is a batching or concurrency limit. The validation metric after the fix is wall time per request and the transfer share of it: success is the copy stage shrinking as a fraction of a falling wall time, with kernel time deliberately left untouched until it actually dominates.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: Copies plus queue wait are ~70% of wall time; kernel math is ~8%, so kernel tuning is premature.
criteria: Transfer and admission cost (11 ms copies plus 6 ms queue) is identified as dominant over the 2 ms kernel.
Low-level kernel tuning is rejected as a premature optimization target given the profile.
The next measurement (split HtoD/DtoH, check resident inputs) and a validation metric (transfer share of a falling wall time) are both proposed.

exerciseSolutions.title: Integrate a GPU worker into an async and distributed service
exerciseSolutions.solution:
Treat the single device as a scarce shared worker behind one bounded queue, and make admission, ownership, retry, and replay policy explicit before the first incident. The pipeline is ingest -> parse -> score on GPU -> persist -> notify, traffic is bursty, there is one device per host, and duplicate replay must stay harmless after crash recovery.

The bounded GPU queue sits at the single admission point in front of the score stage, and it owns the device, the persistent device buffers, and the right to decide what runs next. There is exactly one consumer task draining this queue and driving the one device; async tasks upstream can generate work far faster than a single GPU can absorb it, so the queue is where backpressure lives. When it is full, ingest must slow, shed, or route to a CPU fallback rather than pile unbounded work onto a device that cannot keep up. Making this the one explicit choke point keeps the GPU from being treated as a free fan-out target.

The async side hands over owned data, not borrowed views, at the moment it enqueues. A request-local borrow cannot cross into the GPU worker, because the worker outlives the request task and may hold the payload across awaits and a multi-millisecond round trip; a borrowed buffer that outlives its request is exactly the dangling-reference failure the chapter flags. So parse produces an owned, Send payload (an owned Vec or boxed buffer) and moves it into the queue, transferring ownership to the worker. The worker copies it to the device, runs the kernel, and returns an owned result downstream.

Separate transient GPU retry from terminal failure with a typed error and a budget. Transient conditions (device busy, queue full, a recoverable launch error, a transfer hiccup) are retried a bounded number of times with backoff and may fall back to the CPU path when the retry budget is exhausted; terminal conditions (malformed input, a shape that can never be valid, a persistent device fault) fail the item outright and surface to the caller. Crucially, completion must be idempotent so replay after a crash or lease expiry is harmless: stamp each work item with a stable request id, make persist an upsert keyed by that id, and make notify deduplicate on it, so re-scoring a replayed item produces the same persisted record rather than a double write. Combined with a lease on the in-flight item, a crash mid-score simply lets the item time out and be re-admitted exactly once in effect.

Require observability before rollout, at least: queue age or wait time at the admission point, transfer bytes per request in each direction, launch count per second, and CPU-fallback rate. Add device utilization and per-stage latency so you can tell transfer-bound from launch-bound from genuinely kernel-bound under real load, which is the whole point of refusing to ship the boundary on faith.
exerciseSolutions.codeNote: One bounded queue owns the device; owned jobs cross the boundary; retry, fallback, and idempotent persist are explicit.
criteria: A single bounded admission queue in front of the score stage owns the device and its buffers.
Owned, Send payloads are moved into the worker rather than borrowed request-local views.
Idempotent completion (stable request id, upsert persist, lease) makes crash and lease-expiry replay harmless.
At least three observability hooks are required: queue age, transfer bytes, launch count, and CPU-fallback rate.

device     = NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 Laptop GPU
matrix     = 1024 x 1024 (f32)
cpu        = 116.1 ms
gpu kernel = 2.35 ms
gpu total  = 12.7 ms  (incl. host<->device copies)
speedup    = 49.4x kernel, 9.1x end-to-end

labSolution.explanation:
This is an extended bonus demo that goes beyond the starter lab. The direct answer to the starter lab (`safe_launch_wrapper_lab.rs`, expected output `blocks = 8 / threads = 128 / launch ok = true`) is exercise 3's solution above; this section instead shows what a real GPU offload looks like end to end.

This is the real thing: a CUDA C kernel (a string compiled to PTX at run time by NVRTC) launched through cudarc with one GPU thread per output element, measured against a cache-friendly i-k-j CPU baseline.

The kernel maps `row`/`col` from the 2-D block and grid indices, guards the N x N bounds, accumulates the dot product of A's row and B's column, and writes one C[row*N + col]. The host code copies A and B to the device, launches a 16x16-thread grid sized by `div_ceil(N, 16)`, synchronizes, and copies C back. It times the GPU two ways: the kernel alone, and the end-to-end path including the host<->device copies.

Both numbers matter. The kernel speedup (~50x on an RTX 3080 at N=1024) is what the GPU is capable of; the end-to-end speedup (~9x) is what you actually get once the O(N^2) PCIe transfers are paid for around a single O(N^3) multiply. That gap is the chapter's transfer-budget lesson made concrete: GPU wins scale with compute done per byte moved, so larger matrices — or keeping data resident on the device across many kernels — widen the real-world win. The correctness check (max relative error below 1e-3) confirms the GPU and CPU agree to f32 precision.

reviewAnswers.question: What kinds of workloads actually amortize host-device transfer and launch cost well?
reviewAnswers.answer: Workloads with high arithmetic intensity and a large enough batch: they do a great deal of computation per byte moved across the bus, so the kernel runs long enough to hide the host-to-device and device-to-host copies behind it, and the per-launch fixed cost is spread across many items. Dense, regular, batched math like a large GEMM or a batched tensor operation is the canonical fit. Small, low-intensity, bandwidth-limited work such as a vector add or a tiny per-request transform does not amortize the boundary and usually loses to the CPU, because the copy and launch dominate the trivial arithmetic.

reviewAnswers.question: Why is a safe Rust wrapper around a kernel launch mostly an ownership and invariant story?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because the kernel call itself is one small unsafe operation, and everything dangerous around it is shape and lifetime: matching buffer lengths, nonzero grid and block counts, and device buffers that genuinely outlive the launch. The safe wrapper's job is to check those invariants in ordinary Rust and to own the device buffers so they cannot dangle, returning a Result that names any failure, leaving the unsafe block to do nothing but the launch. In C++ host code these invariants live in convention and review comments, where a mismatched length is silent corruption; Rust moves them into the type system and the wrapper, so the GPU boundary follows the same FFI discipline used elsewhere in the book.

reviewAnswers.question: What is the practical difference between host memory ownership and device memory ownership?
reviewAnswers.answer: Host memory and device memory are two separate domains with separate allocators, and a pointer into one is meaningless in the other; a Vec<T> on the host is not addressable by the kernel, and a device buffer is not addressable by host code. So a device allocation needs its own owner whose Drop frees the device memory, distinct from any host Vec, and data only crosses between them through an explicit copy. The practical consequence is that the host wrapper must decide when device buffers exist and when they disappear, and must never let a kernel hold a pointer into host memory or into a device buffer that has already been freed.

reviewAnswers.question: Why are queue wait and launch count often more useful than one isolated kernel timing?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because a kernel-only profile cannot tell you whether you are transfer-bound, launch-bound, queue-bound, or actually kernel-bound, and in service code the kernel is usually the cheapest stage. A high launch count with microsecond kernels signals a launch-bound path that wants batching or fusion, and a large queue wait signals an admission or concurrency limit in front of the device, neither of which a fast kernel time would reveal. Wall time should drive the first question; breaking it into named stages (queue, copy, launch, kernel, sync) tells you which cost to attack and keeps you from tuning arithmetic that was never the bottleneck.

reviewAnswers.question: When is CUDA the wrong choice even when a kernel itself is efficient?
reviewAnswers.answer: When the surrounding system, not the kernel, dominates the cost: the work is too small to amortize the transfer and launch, the path launches too many tiny kernels, it copies too much across the bus, or one shared device has no admission control and becomes a contention point. An efficient kernel does not help if each request pays a full round trip and a synchronize for a trivial payload, which is the tiny-kernel service that loses to the CPU. In those cases the right answer is to batch, fuse, cache resident inputs, or keep the route on the CPU entirely, because the failure is a systems and ownership problem, not a kernel one.

reviewAnswers.question: Why should device memory be modeled as an explicit owner handle rather than a borrowed pointer into host memory?
reviewAnswers.answer: Because host and device memory are two separate domains with separate allocators, so a pointer into host memory is meaningless to the kernel and a device address is meaningless to host code. A borrowed pointer also carries no ownership of the device allocation, so nothing frees that residency when the borrow ends and nothing prevents the host buffer it points at from moving or dropping out from under an in-flight launch. Modeling the device buffer as its own owner handle that allocates on construction and frees the device memory on Drop ties residency to a Rust value the host controls, makes the lifetime of device memory explicit and distinct from any host Vec, and lets the wrapper decide exactly when buffers exist, when they are reused, and when they disappear. That is the same ownership discipline the safe launch wrapper depends on to guarantee buffers outlive the launch.
